fatal_errors: The proposed CoCrFeNi-Ti-Zr precipitation-treatment strategy does not reconstruct the target composition-screening method in the refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system.

None of the cited evidence establishes that approximately 2 at.% Ti and 1 at.% Zr in CoCrFeNi will form coherent Ni3Ti-type precipitates together with beneficial short-range order after the specified 600 °C treatment.

The claimed ductility and fracture-toughness improvements are not supported by the cited precipitation-strengthening studies, which primarily demonstrate strength retention or strength-ductility balance in different chemistries.
The falsification rule is overly conjunctive: failure to meet a central mechanical prediction could avoid falsification if the proposed microstructure is nevertheless observed.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad structural-HEA goal and proposes measurable mechanical and microstructural tests, but it is scientifically remote from the hidden target. The target used validated rule-of-mixtures modulus estimates, VEC, and density to screen 38,326 Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W compositions and selected Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 for room-temperature as-cast compression. Its mechanism concerned reduced VEC, a lower Peierls–Nabarro barrier, enhanced dislocation slip, and delayed brittle cracking. The generated hypothesis instead introduces an unvalidated heat treatment and precipitation/SRO mechanism in an FCC CoCrFeNi-derived alloy. The evidence supports coherent ordered nanoprecipitates as a general strengthening concept, particularly Ni3Al-type precipitates in other alloys, but not the proposed chemistry, Ni3Ti phase, processing window, SRO behavior, modulus retention, or numerical toughness and ductility gains. The experiment is reasonably testable, yet it needs composition-matched untreated and treatment-only controls and separate falsification thresholds for microstructure, strength, ductility, toughness, and modulus.
